title: Rollout handoff latency profiles for quantized model variants - spot diary
body:
Summary:
This is a short, focused diary of an exploratory investigation into micro-latency spikes observed during rolling deploys where we switch between quantized model variants (e.g., AWQ-int8 -> FP8 fallback). The goal: surface the handoff mechanics that cause transient p95/p99 jumps and produce reproducible checks we can run in staging before a live rollout.

Motivation / observed symptom:
- On a recent canary rollout of an AWQ-int8 variant, we saw intermittent p99 spikes (+2.4x baseline) clustered around the time servers were marked active for the new variant.
- Spikes last 150–700ms (per-request extra latency) and correlated with elevated kernel swap/selection counts and cache misses on KV cache.
- Not consistent with steady-state quantized performance (steady-state benchmarks look fine).

Hypotheses (what might be happening):
1) Kernel selection jitter: the dispatcher briefly probes multiple kernels (fallback path) and incurs extra scheduling overhead when routing to newly-registered variant instances.
2) KV cache coldness on the new variant: new model instances don't share warmed KV cache and initial requests suffer warmup; redeploys amplify this effect.
3) Small burst contention on the CUDA streams when new model weights are loaded and a GPU memory compaction/eviction happens.
4) Routing jitter from traffic shaper toggling between variants faster than warmup completes.

Quick reproducibility plan (staging):
- Use replay harness (linked in artifacts) with synthetic traffic matching production QPS+burst profile.
- Two variants: model-A (AWQ-int8 optimized kernels) and model-B (FP8 fallback kernels).
- Start with 100% model-B running warm for 30m, then ramp canary traffic to 5% model-A over 5m. Observe tail latencies. Repeat with inverse direction.
- Capture: per-request trace with kernel-id, kernel-switch count, kv-cache-hit bool, gpu-mem-eviction events.

Commands/bench notes:
- replay run --config=handoff-staging.yaml --qps=350 --burst=1.8x --duration=20m
- collect traces to /tmp/handoff-traces-<run>.json, then run `hand-off-analyze` (internal tool) to join traces with host/driver metrics.

Key metrics to log:
- p50/p95/p99 request latencies (overall and split by kernel-id)
- kernel-switch count per-request (how many different kernel implementations executed)
- KV cache hit ratio (prefix hits) during handoff window
- GPU mem compact/eviction counts and host OOM indicators
- Time between variant activation and first request served by that instance

Findings (from two quick runs on 2026-06-15 and 2026-06-20):
Run A (AWQ-int8 canary into FP8 baseline):
- p99 jumped from 210ms -> 520ms during 90s window after canary activation.
- 48% of p99 requests had kernel-switch count >1 (common case: dispatcher attempted fast-path AWQ kernel, failed heuristic, retried FP8 kernel).
- KV cache miss rate on new instances: 87% for first 5 requests, then decayed.
- GPU mem-compaction spikes aligned with model load on 2 hosts; those hosts showed an extra 80–300ms per affected request.

Run B (FP8 -> AWQ-int8):
- p99 jump smaller (210ms -> 330ms) but more frequent micro-spikes (100–250ms) across 3m window.
- Kernel-switch >1 for 22% p99 requests (less than A), but the dispatcher consumed extra CPU cycles when evaluating kernel heuristics (visible on host CPU profilers).
- No mem-eviction in this direction; KV misses still present but slightly lower (first-request miss 70%).

Interpretation / short takeaways:
- Combination of dispatcher kernel-probing + cold KV cache explains most of the long tail during the first 1–3 minutes of a canary activation.
- GPU memory events amplify tail when model weights are loaded concurrently with traffic – avoid concurrent load + ramp.
- The difference between A and B suggests AWQ->FP8 path triggers more aggressive fallback behavior (probing sequence longer) than FP8->AWQ. Might be historical heuristic ordering.

Quick mitigations to try in staging before wide rollouts:
1) Stagger model activation: mark instances ACTIVE only after a warmup ping protocol (prefetch KV prefixes and run a short warmup trace).
2) Dispatcher change: add a short-lived sticky kernel binding during first N requests to avoid repeated probing per-request. (config flag: kernel.probe_window_ms)
3) Limit parallel model loads during rolling upgrades (coordination in release-engineering) to avoid mem-compaction overlap.
4) Add pre-warm job when deploying new quantized variants that primes KV caches across pool.

Experiment TODOs (next 2 weeks):
- Implement and test sticky-kernel-binding flag on a small staging canary (owner: Diego).
- Add prewarm hook to rollout pipeline and measure reduction in p99 during handoff (owner: Samir).
- Instrument dispatcher to emit kernel-probe latency histogram and make it visible in Console as a per-rollout metric (owner: Claire).

Open questions / risks:
- Does sticky binding increase long-term latency for certain instruction distributions? Need microbench to ensure no regression.
- Are there workloads that depend on per-request kernel switching for correctness (rare but check specialized kernels)?
- Prewarming increases deploy time and temporary cost; need to balance against SLA risk.

Notes-to-self / loose logs:
- Attach trace snippets in `linked_artifacts` PR once sanitized (sensitive host ids removed).
- Cross-ref with `confluence.redwood/internal/warmup-strategies` for prewarm implementation patterns.

Appendix (raw micro-observations):
- Example trace: request id X -> kernel_try AWQ_int8 (120ms), retry FP8_kernel (230ms) -> total 350ms; kv_cache_miss=true; gpu_eviction=false.
- Example trace with mem eviction: request id Y -> model weight swap started 50ms before RPC arrived; extra 210ms on GPU; top processes show compaction thread 85% cpu.

If useful, I can convert this diary into a short playbook with exact gating checks for rollout pipelines (prewarm thresholds, acceptable p99 delta, and automated rollback triggers).

-- Claire
